en: He devastated the Kyzylbash realm
And made its girls and women weep.
No land remained anywhere
That the racehorse Akkula had not trodden;
No people remained whole
Who had not heard his battle cry.
He broke through Ombu and opened a road,
And took booty from many lands.
He entered the Caliph's court and received a writ,
And received a blessing from the prince.
He raised strife in many lands,
And throughout Kakan and Beijing
He came to be called blood-drinking Manas.
Kongurbay, son of Alooke,
Without even racing Algara,
Had taken the prize away;
The merciless turmoil
Had then been set in motion.
When Akkula was entered in the race,
Your gray-wolf lion Manas
Was left with nothing.
The hero Manas lamented:
"Accursed, faithless world—
Why did I have to find you,
Foal of the bay mare,
Fleetest of the black herd,
Akkula, whom I ride into battle—
Why did I insist on racing him?
The black Chinese and the Manchus—
Their prowess, before my own eyes,
I had held for nothing;
That blood-drinker, the infidel Kongurbay,
That hero whose wrath is full,
Would enter this joust—
I had failed to understand it."
While Manas stood speaking thus,
His thoughts, it seemed, were divided.
Kanykei, the gray wolf's wife,
Appeared like the whole world,
Kanykei, mistress of every craft,
Showing the whiteness beneath her chin,
Her white breast gleaming,
Spoke softly and said this.
Having caused much bustle,
She finished it that very day.
The blood-drinker's Akolpok armor
She lifted up then
And had it brought to Akayar.
Beauty of the dark-bay folk,
Radiance of the Muslims,
Most graceful of the long-haired,
Most excellent of women:
"It would be wrong not to prepare," she said.
"My hero, my wolf, my sultan,
If he meets the Kalmyk face to face,
Might he come to harm?" she thought.
From scraps and bits of material,
Kanykei had spent six years
Making the Akolpok armor.
Its lining was velvet, its outside calico,
And it was half a cubit thick.
Your formidable sister-in-law Kanykei
Had the lands from Orol-Tobo to Margalang,
And all the country between,
Supply her with the cotton fiber,
Which she had brought by Kembai.
Its collar was gold and its sleeves were brass,
With paired mail rings like lark's eyes;
A wide coat with a broad collar,
When worn in battle no bullet pierced it.
The point of a spear could not puncture it,
Nor could an armor-cutting arrow pass through.
The matchless Akolpok armor
Was supple as a snake's belly;
Those who looked at it were amazed,
And people's eyes slid from its sheen.
Its lining was packed with tempered steel;
When she bent that dark metal,
Many awls made of steel
Were snapped in two.
She had its weak places hammered,
Had damask steel filed down,
And poured into its middle.
Around the outside she wrapped silk.
While the Akolpok was being made,
Much of your gray wolf's treasury
Was spent away.
Between its layers of dark metal
She placed every kind of tempered steel.
When the hero donned it and girded himself,
Any mortal who faced him withered.
Burning buckthorn could not scorch it,
And a shot from Akkelte could not pierce it.
"My hero, his father's only son,
Must stand wearing the Akolpok,
So when there is a shouting enemy,
He may throw himself forward without fear.
I cannot leave this undone;
If I do not perform this service,
My labor will never prosper.
The Akolpok you now see—
I could not rest until I made it;
How could I ever live at ease?" she said.
She had twisted its warp with care.
At Kokotoy's memorial feast,
Before the vast assembly,
"He will be killed if they joust," she thought,
And knew it from the very beginning.
She repaired every weak place
And prepared it for the joust
At Kokotoy's great spectacle.
Before all the people, Kanykei
Showed what a wife she was;
She brought Khan Manas's Akolpok
And placed it upon him.
The capable wife Kanykei
Showed the skill of her hands.
Its ties numbered nine;
On the prince's inner side
She had them fastened crosswise.
Its buttons numbered nine;
She closed all its buttons,
Fitting them across the breast
Of the prince who loomed like a mountain.
Her voice fell mournfully
As, over the noble steed,
The gray sash that fell from the sky,
Over the Akolpok armor,
She buckled around Khan Manas:
"Recognize this as my service;
Go against the enemy without fear.
Though I may be a proud, haughty woman,
Know the worth I bear.
Many souls face deep regret;
If you wear the Akolpok,
It will be of great use in war.
If you raise a mighty clash with the Chinese,
When infidel and Muslim
Come together in bitter struggle,
May my panther prince wear it,
And understand my worth.
At night I went without sleep,
By day I had no rest;
I crafted its precious lining
And worked it with my teeth for many years.
Gnawing at the dark metal,
I wore my shovel-like teeth away;
Staring as I worked the dark metal,
I dimmed my black eyes.
I twisted its warp eighty times,
Thinking of every place
My lion prince and panther might go.
Thinking it was the tree planted for Talas,
Thinking it was the hour
My lion prince and sultan would clash,
I went on making the Akolpok.
Kongurbay, son of Alooke,
Would bring torment to this feast—
I knew that they would fight."
Telling her grief, Kanykei
Moved all the watching people to sorrow;
Upon the lion hero
She placed the Akolpok armor,
And Kanykei remained watching.
"She is truly the khan's wife," they said,
And the people's lament was this:
"This woman Kanykei—
That astonishing woman of perfect wisdom—
Beneath her skirt has ten heads,
And thimbles seem to move there.
Had any man but Khan Manas lived,
He would never have taken a wife,
But would have remained a bachelor.
Whenever it was, Khan Manas
Was carried away by his valor;
The panther met Kanykei
When she was fourteen years old.
She is truly a holy handmaiden;
Her meeting with Khan Manas
Was one of the nights of sacred destiny.
The poor woman, almost a saint—
One cannot speak of her like that.
Whoever speaks of her so,
His affairs will never prosper.
She met him in her youth,
And splendid Manas
She built up like a house,
She tended like a garden,
Raised him to maturity and made him a man;
Matchless Manas
She made the equal of every hero's son.
Kanykei never disgraces herself;
She turns her lofty head into a standard,
And a woman's head into a warrior's.
Making armor is her custom;
At all times Kanykei
Is this Manas's wing.
This wondrous Kanykei
Was given by almighty Allah
To Manas himself—
A woman like a heavenly maiden.
Lion Manas gathered his strength
And donned the Akolpok armor;
Kalkaman's Black Horse
He sprang upon without a saddle.
The people surged together,
And stared at Manas in wonder.
The twelve Muslim khans
The boundless gray-wolf panther
Made equal among themselves.
To choose a swift horse to ride,
To go against Kongurbay,
The Muslims' horses
Were led out in a long line.
They brought saintly Bakai
To judge the horses.
The great host of dark-clad Muslims,
Its champions, filed past;
The splendid host of Muslims
All filed past together.
Dark native-bred chargers,
With bellows lungs and copper forelegs—
Every one of the thoroughbreds
Bakai examined in turn.
At Kokotoy's memorial feast
A vast multitude had gathered.
If they met chest to chest in a joust,
No horse there could endure it.
Khan Manas's forty companions,
His forty companions, forty comrades,
Each of the forty had his own distinction;
The forty were master riders
Who had come from forty lands.
Manas the blessed panther
Gathered his forty companions,
And before your elder Bakai
Had them lead their horses past.
At the sound of tumult it stood apart:
Almambet's Sarala
Showed every mark of a thoroughbred.
It never panicked at a battle cry,
And in the darkness of the moonless night
Never once set a hoof wrong;
It showed every mark of a thoroughbred.
No horse appeared that could bend it
When ridden out into a joust;
No horse appeared that could make it yield
When they stood chest to chest.
Almambet's Sarala,
With mattock hooves and broad hindquarters,
Was a beast to ride into battle.
With bowl-shaped hooves and a broad back,
Almambet's Sarala
Was a beast to ride in a race.
With camel chest and low mane,
It was a beast to ride into combat.
